# Inductive Logic

One of the most successfully cultivated branches of philosophy in our time is what is called inductive logic, the study of the conditions under which our sciences have evolved.[^1] Writers on this subject have begun to show a singular unanimity as to what the laws of nature and elements of fact mean, when formulated by mathematicians, physicists and chemists.[^2]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "One of the most successfully cultivated branches of philosophy in our time is what is called inductive logic, the study of the conditions under which our sciences have evolved."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Writers on this subject have begun to show a singular unanimity as to what the laws of nature and elements of fact mean, when formulated by mathematicians, physicists and chemists."

# Men Believed Laws Deciphered the Thoughts of the Almighty

When the first mathematical, logical and natural uniformities, the first LAWS, were discovered, men were so carried away by the clearness, beauty and simplification that resulted, that they believed themselves to have deciphered authentically the eternal thoughts of the Almighty.[^1]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "When the first mathematical, logical and natural uniformities, the first LAWS, were discovered, men were so carried away by the clearness, beauty and simplification that resulted, that they believed themselves to have deciphered authentically the eternal thoughts of the Almighty."

# Laws Are Only Approximations

But as the sciences have developed farther, the notion has gained ground that most, perhaps all, of our laws are only approximations.[^1] The laws themselves, moreover, have grown so numerous that there is no counting them; and so many rival formulations are proposed in all the branches of science that investigators have become accustomed to the notion that no theory is absolutely a transcript of reality, but that any one of them may from some point of view be useful.[^2] Their great use is to summarize old facts and to lead to new ones.[^3] They are only a man-made language, a conceptual shorthand, as someone calls them, in which we write our reports of nature; and languages, as is well known, tolerate much choice of expression and many dialects.[^4]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "But as the sciences have developed farther, the notion has gained ground that most, perhaps all, of our laws are only approximations."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "The laws themselves, moreover, have grown so numerous that there is no counting them; and so many rival formulations are proposed in all the branches of science that investigators have become accustomed to the notion that no theory is absolutely a transcript of reality, but that any one of them may from some point of view be useful."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Their great use is to summarize old facts and to lead to new ones."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "They are only a man-made language, a conceptual shorthand, as someone calls them, in which we write our reports of nature; and languages, as is well known, tolerate much choice of expression and many dialects."

# Human Arbitrariness Has Driven Divine Necessity from Scientific Logic

Thus human arbitrariness has driven divine necessity from scientific logic.[^1]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Thus human arbitrariness has driven divine necessity from scientific logic."
=== FILE: Ideas Become True Just in So Far as They Help Us.md ===

# Ideas Become True Just in So Far as They Help Us

Riding now on the front of this wave of scientific logic Messrs.[^1] Schiller and Dewey appear with their pragmatistic account of what truth everywhere signifies.[^2] Everywhere, these teachers say, 'truth' in our ideas and beliefs means the same thing that it means in science.[^3] It means, they say, nothing but this, THAT IDEAS (WHICH THEMSELVES ARE BUT PARTS OF OUR EXPERIENCE) BECOME TRUE JUST IN SO FAR AS THEY HELP US TO GET INTO SATISFACTORY RELATION WITH OTHER PARTS OF OUR EXPERIENCE, to summarize them and get about among them by conceptual short-cuts instead of following the interminable succession of particular phenomena.[^4]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Riding now on the front of this wave of scientific logic Messrs."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Schiller and Dewey appear with their pragmatistic account of what truth everywhere signifies."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Everywhere, these teachers say, 'truth' in our ideas and beliefs means the same thing that it means in science."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "It means, they say, nothing but this, THAT IDEAS (WHICH THEMSELVES ARE BUT PARTS OF OUR EXPERIENCE) BECOME TRUE JUST IN SO FAR AS THEY HELP US TO GET INTO SATISFACTORY RELATION WITH OTHER PARTS OF OUR EXPERIENCE, to summarize them and get about among them by conceptual short-cuts instead of following the interminable succession of particular phenomena."
=== FILE: The Instrumental View of Truth.md ===

aliases: []

---

# The Instrumental View of Truth

Any idea upon which we can ride, so to speak; any idea that will carry us prosperously from any one part of our experience to any other part, linking things satisfactorily, working securely, simplifying, saving labor; is true for just so much, true in so far forth, true INSTRUMENTALLY.[^1] This is the 'instrumental' view of truth taught so successfully at Chicago, the view that truth in our ideas means their power to 'work,' promulgated so brilliantly at Oxford.[^2]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Any idea upon which we can ride, so to speak; any idea that will carry us prosperously from any one part of our experience to any other part, linking things satisfactorily, working securely, simplifying, saving labor; is true for just so much, true in so far forth, true INSTRUMENTALLY."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "This is the 'instrumental' view of truth taught so successfully at Chicago, the view that truth in our ideas means their power to 'work,' promulgated so brilliantly at Oxford."

# Following the Example of Geologists, Biologists and Philologists

Messrs.[^1] Dewey, Schiller and their allies, in reaching this general conception of all truth, have only followed the example of geologists, biologists and philologists.[^2] In the establishment of these other sciences, the successful stroke was always to take some simple process actually observable in operation[^3] and then to generalize it, making it apply to all times, and produce great results by summating its effects through the ages.[^4]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Messrs."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "Dewey, Schiller and their allies, in reaching this general conception of all truth, have only followed the example of geologists, biologists and philologists."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "In the establishment of these other sciences, the successful stroke was always to take some simple process actually observable in operation"
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#Pragmatism as a Theory of Truth]] "and then to generalize it, making it apply to all times, and produce great results by summating its effects through the ages."
